strengths: The paper identifies a concrete and plausible failure mode of reverse-KL on-policy distillation: mode-seeking behavior can under-preserve high-entropy teacher distributions. The proposed EOPD objective is simple, well motivated, and easy to integrate into PPO-style OPD pipelines.

The empirical section is reasonably broad for this topic: results are reported for three Qwen3 student sizes, six math benchmarks, several OOD benchmarks, entropy-driven baselines, threshold ablations, placement ablations, and an additional Llama-family experiment in the appendix.

The paper provides useful diagnostic evidence beyond final accuracy, including token-level entropy histograms and forward-KL measurements on high-entropy teacher positions. These analyses help connect the method to its intended mechanism.

Implementation details are better than average: the manuscript specifies major hyperparameters, training datasets, rollout settings, sampling settings, top-k approximation, prompt templates, and evaluation protocols.
weaknesses: The central empirical gains are modest and not supported by statistical uncertainty. Several benchmarks are small, especially AIME24/25, and the paper reports no confidence intervals, bootstrap tests, multiple training seeds, or variance over sampling. Some claimed improvements could plausibly be noise.

The novelty is incremental. EOPD is essentially reverse-KL OPD plus a top-k forward-KL term gated by teacher entropy. This is a sensible engineering idea, but the paper does not sufficiently distinguish it from existing mixed-divergence, generalized KD, entropy-aware, or adaptive distillation methods beyond surface-level related work.

The ablation against full forward KL weakens the main claim. Full forward KL is often competitive with EOPD and even better on some Pass@8 metrics, so the evidence does not clearly establish that entropy-aware placement is essential rather than merely a compute-saving heuristic.

The toy experiment is not very convincing as evidence for LLM training instability. The top-10-restricted categorical student, single-logit update rule, and selected top-k change metrics are quite far from the PPO-style LLM objective, and the setup appears designed to make high-entropy teachers look unstable.

The paper does not adequately quantify efficiency. Since EOPD requires querying teacher entropy and top-k probabilities for token positions, the claimed preservation of on-policy efficiency needs wall-clock, memory, teacher-query, and throughput comparisons against OPD, full forward KL, and KD.

Evaluation is narrow in task type and teacher/student setting. Most main results use Qwen3-8B as teacher and math-oriented training/evaluation; the Llama appendix is small. It is unclear whether the method helps outside reasoning-heavy math domains or with larger teacher-student gaps.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful hyperparameter tables. The manuscript does not mention code release, exact random seeds, exact dataset preprocessing/splits, checkpoint selection, hardware, total compute, or how contamination was handled for math benchmarks.

Limitations and ethics are treated too briefly. The impact statement says no new ethical concerns are identified, but the paper does not discuss risks of distilling teacher errors, calibration failures from preserving uncertainty, benchmark contamination, or deployment misuse of stronger smaller models.

strengths: The paper identifies a plausible weakness of reverse-KL on-policy distillation: mode-seeking updates can underrepresent high-entropy teacher distributions. This is a relevant issue for reasoning models where multiple continuations may be valid.

The proposed method is simple and practical: add a top-k forward-KL term only at token positions where teacher entropy exceeds a threshold. This is easy to implement in existing OPD/PPO-style pipelines and has modest overhead.

The empirical section is reasonably broad for a systems-style distillation paper: three Qwen student sizes, several math benchmarks, some OOD evaluation, entropy-driven baselines, threshold ablations, and an additional Llama-family appendix experiment.
Presentation is generally clear. The motivation, algorithm, and experimental setup are understandable, and the paper includes useful hyperparameter details for KD, OPD, EOPD, and GRPO.
weaknesses: Soundness is the main concern. The central claim that entropy-aware placement is essential is only weakly supported. In Table 6, full forward KL is competitive with EOPD and even matches or exceeds it on some Pass@8 metrics, so the evidence does not convincingly isolate the benefit of entropy-based gating over simply adding forward KL more broadly.

The reported gains are often small and not accompanied by statistical testing or multiple training seeds. On AIME benchmarks, many changes correspond to one or two problems, and several results are ties or regressions. Without variance estimates, the claimed consistent improvements are not reliable enough.

The toy experiment is not very persuasive evidence for LLM training behavior. It uses a hand-designed categorical distribution, top-10 sampling constraint, and a simplified single-logit update; this illustrates an intuition but does not establish that reverse-KL instability is the operative cause of the observed benchmark differences.

Several experimental choices confound interpretation. Different training datasets are used across model sizes, the main comparisons emphasize OPD while GRPO or KD are sometimes competitive or better, and OOD evaluation is only reported for one model size. The paper does not clearly separate benefits from better uncertainty transfer, extra teacher supervision, hyperparameter choices, or compute differences.

Originality is limited. Entropy-gated interpolation between reverse-KL and forward-KL objectives is a natural extension of known mode-seeking/mode-covering KL behavior, and the paper does not sufficiently distinguish itself from prior generalized/on-policy distillation methods beyond this heuristic.

Reproducibility is partial but incomplete. Hyperparameters and frameworks are listed, but there is no code release, no seed information, no compute budget, no exact training data preprocessing details, and no discussion of how teacher top-k probabilities/logits are stored or queried at scale beyond a brief memory plot.

The limitations and ethics discussion is thin. The impact statement largely says there are no new ethical concerns, but the method targets stronger deployable reasoning models and should discuss risks such as amplifying teacher errors, benchmark contamination, misuse of distilled capabilities, and environmental cost of teacher querying.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence, especially phrases such as demonstrating that accounting for teacher uncertainty is essential. The results suggest it may help in this setup, but the paper does not establish necessity or broad generality.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and practically relevant failure mode of reverse-KL on-policy distillation: mode-seeking behavior can under-transfer teacher uncertainty at high-entropy token positions. The motivation is well connected to reasoning tasks where multiple continuations may be valid.

The proposed EOPD objective is simple, well specified, and easy to integrate into existing OPD/PPO-style pipelines: use clipped reverse KL generally, and add a top-k forward KL term when teacher entropy exceeds a threshold.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad for this topic, covering three Qwen student sizes, six math benchmarks, out-of-domain evaluations on GPQA-Diamond, MMLU-Pro, and AlpacaEval, entropy-based baselines, threshold ablations, forward-KL placement ablations, and an additional Llama-family appendix.

Results are directionally consistent: EOPD usually improves over OPD, with especially meaningful Pass@8 gains at larger scale, and the entropy/forward-KL analyses support the intended mechanism rather than only reporting end-task scores.
Presentation is generally clear. The preliminaries, objective, algorithm, and ablation structure make the contribution understandable and reproducible in broad outline.
weaknesses: The main contribution is incremental: entropy-gated addition of forward KL to an on-policy reverse-KL baseline is intuitive and useful, but not a major algorithmic departure from existing KL-mixing, generalized distillation, or entropy-aware exploration ideas.

Several gains are modest or inconsistent at the per-benchmark level. For example, EOPD does not uniformly beat OPD on every Avg@8/Pass@8 entry, and some AIME results are based on very small benchmark sizes where a few examples can change conclusions substantially.

The paper lacks uncertainty estimates for the main LLM experiments. Apart from the toy experiment, there are no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results, making it hard to assess the statistical reliability of the reported 1-2 point average gains.

The efficiency claim is not fully demonstrated. The method is motivated as preserving OPD efficiency, but there are no wall-clock, FLOP, memory, or teacher-query comparisons against OPD, full forward KL, or GRPO beyond a top-k memory analysis.

Reproducibility is only partial. Hyperparameters and evaluation settings are provided, but important details such as exact dataset preprocessing, number of training steps, random seeds, hardware, checkpoint selection, and code/model release plans are missing or underspecified.

The analysis of high-entropy tokens is suggestive but not fully causal. The paper shows that EOPD better matches teacher distributions in high-entropy regions, but does not directly establish which types of reasoning decisions benefit, nor whether teacher entropy is always a reliable proxy for useful diversity rather than ambiguity/noise.

Limitations are not discussed in a dedicated or sufficiently candid way. The impact statement is present, but there is little treatment of failure cases, added teacher-computation cost, sensitivity to teacher calibration, possible benchmark contamination, or risks from distilling undesirable teacher behavior.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant weakness of on-policy distillation for LLM reasoning: reverse-KL objectives can be overly mode-seeking, especially where the teacher has genuine uncertainty. The proposed fix is simple and well motivated: retain clipped reverse-KL on ordinary tokens and add a top-k forward-KL term only at high-teacher-entropy positions.

The empirical evaluation is broader than many distillation papers: three Qwen3 student sizes, six math benchmarks, pass@k curves, out-of-domain checks, Llama-family validation, and ablations over entropy threshold, forward-KL coefficient, top-k, KL placement, GKD, entropy bonuses, and adaptive KL baselines.

The efficiency story is plausible and useful. The paper quantifies the added cost of selective forward KL, reporting about 4.5% step-time overhead and substantially less memory than applying forward KL everywhere.

Presentation is generally clear. The method is easy to understand, the algorithm is explicit, and the appendices include many relevant implementation details such as batch sizes, learning rates, rollout settings, templates, and evaluation prompts.
weaknesses: The central empirical gains are modest and sometimes inconsistent at the individual benchmark/metric level. Several rows show ties or worse performance than OPD or other baselines, while the paper’s prose sometimes overstates the consistency of improvements. No confidence intervals, statistical tests, or multi-seed runs are reported for the main LLM experiments, which is important given small benchmarks such as AIME and differences of only a few percentage points.

The mechanistic claim that reverse KL gives unstable learning signals in high-entropy regions is not fully established. The toy experiment uses a highly simplified categorical setup with a top-10 capacity restriction and a nonstandard update, so it is suggestive rather than decisive. The LLM entropy histograms compare entropy on generated trajectories and may confound model uncertainty with different sampled contexts.

Originality is moderate. Entropy-aware or adaptive KL weighting has substantial related precedent, including methods based on entropy gaps, head-tail mismatch, vocabulary discrepancy, entropy bonuses, and GKD-style mixtures. The paper’s specific teacher-entropy routing in on-policy distillation is useful, but the conceptual novelty is incremental rather than transformative.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful hyperparameter details. The abstract says code is publicly available but the link appears blank in the manuscript. The paper does not clearly report random seeds, variance across runs, exact dataset filtering/decontamination, or all baseline tuning details needed to reproduce the reported small gains.

Limitations and ethics are underdeveloped. The impact statement is generic and says no new ethical concerns are identified, but the paper does not seriously discuss limitations such as dependence on teacher quality/calibration, possible amplification of teacher biases or mistakes, sensitivity to entropy calibration across model families, or applicability outside math-heavy reasoning tasks.

strengths: The paper identifies a plausible and practically relevant issue in on-policy distillation: reverse-KL objectives can be overly mode-seeking and may fail to preserve teacher uncertainty at ambiguous token positions.
The proposed method is simple and easy to integrate: add a teacher-entropy-gated forward-KL term, approximated over top-k teacher tokens, while retaining the clipped reverse-KL on-policy objective.

The empirical section is fairly broad in surface area, covering multiple Qwen student sizes, several math benchmarks, OOD evaluations, entropy-based baselines, GKD, full/random forward-KL placement, Llama-family experiments, and hyperparameter ablations.
The paper includes useful implementation details, including training hyperparameters, decoding settings, approximate overhead, and memory comparisons for selective versus full forward KL.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are not strongly supported. Many reported gains are small and inconsistent: EOPD is not uniformly better than OPD or GRPO across Table 2, and on small datasets such as AIME, differences of 3.33 percentage points correspond to roughly one problem. The paper reports no confidence intervals, no repeated runs, and no significance testing, so it is hard to distinguish method effects from sampling/training variance.

The toy experiment in Section 3.2 is not convincing evidence for reverse-KL instability in LLM distillation. It uses an artificial categorical setup, restricts the student to top-10 sampling, and applies a simplified sampled-logit update rather than a faithful policy-gradient or PPO-style reverse-KL optimizer. The observed top-k churn may be an artifact of this setup rather than a general property of reverse KL under high teacher entropy.

The novelty is limited. Entropy-aware or discrepancy-aware adaptive KL distillation is already closely related to cited work such as BD-KD, AKL, ToDi, entropy bonus, advantage shaping, and GKD. The paper positions EOPD as a simple variant but does not provide enough conceptual or theoretical insight to make the contribution feel clearly distinct beyond the particular gating heuristic.

The entropy analysis does not establish causality. The paper shows that EOPD has more high-entropy tokens and lower forward KL in selected regions, but it does not demonstrate that these quantities cause downstream gains rather than merely correlating with the added forward-KL regularizer. The connection between token entropy histograms and reasoning diversity remains mostly asserted.

Baseline fairness is somewhat unclear. GRPO uses eight rollouts per prompt while OPD/EOPD use one rollout, different chat templates are used for distillation versus GRPO, and the 4B model is trained on a different dataset from the smaller models. These choices may be reasonable, but they complicate the interpretation of cross-method and cross-scale comparisons.

The method depends on absolute teacher entropy thresholds, but calibration, temperature, vocabulary/tokenization, and model family can substantially affect entropy values. The paper provides threshold ablations, but does not deeply analyze robustness across teachers, decoding settings, or entropy calibration regimes.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract says the code is publicly available but no URL is provided. The paper lacks random seeds, variance across runs, exact training step counts in the main text, precise dataset filtering/decontamination details, and enough information to reproduce the evaluation variance-sensitive Pass@k results reliably.

The presentation overstates consistency and strength. Several tables show mixed or marginal results, yet the narrative repeatedly describes consistent improvements and essentiality of teacher uncertainty. The limitations section is effectively absent, and the impact statement is generic.

strengths: The paper identifies a concrete and practically relevant failure mode of reverse-KL on-policy distillation: mode-seeking behavior degrades token-level diversity and alignment especially at high teacher-entropy positions. The entropy histogram analysis, toy experiment, and high-entropy forward-KL curves provide a coherent mechanistic motivation for the method.

The proposed EOPD objective is simple, well motivated, and easy to integrate into existing OPD/PPO-style pipelines: retain clipped reverse KL generally and add top-k forward KL only when teacher entropy exceeds a threshold. This gives the work practical value despite the conceptual simplicity.

The empirical evaluation is broad and mostly convincing. The authors test three Qwen3 student sizes on six math reasoning benchmarks, include OOD results on GPQA-Diamond, MMLU-Pro, and AlpacaEval, and add a Llama-family experiment in the appendix. EOPD generally improves over OPD, KD, and GRPO, with especially meaningful Pass@8 gains for larger students.

The ablation suite is strong. The paper compares reverse KL, forward KL, full forward KL, random forward KL, entropy bonus, advantage shaping, GKD variants, and adaptive KL baselines, and studies threshold, coefficient, and top-k sensitivity. These experiments support the claim that where forward KL is applied matters, not merely adding entropy or extra KL regularization.

Reproducibility is reasonably addressed through algorithmic detail, hyperparameter tables, training/evaluation settings, compute overhead measurements, and implementation frameworks. The reported overhead is modest, which strengthens the practical case for the method.
The presentation is clear overall. The paper cleanly separates motivation, method, main results, and supporting analyses, and the figures/tables generally make the empirical story easy to follow.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. The method is a straightforward entropy-gated interpolation of reverse and forward KL with top-k truncation. The contribution is useful, but it is closer to a well-executed objective-selection heuristic than a major conceptual advance.

Some central explanatory claims are stronger than the evidence fully supports. The paper argues that high-entropy teacher tokens correspond to meaningful reasoning decision points, but the evidence is mostly indirect through entropy histograms and downstream benchmark gains. A qualitative or causal analysis of these tokens would make the interpretation more convincing.

The reported gains, while consistent on average, are sometimes modest or mixed at the benchmark level. For example, EOPD ties or underperforms OPD/other baselines on some Avg@8 or Pass@8 entries, including AIME25 for Qwen3-1.7B and some Minerva/OlympiadBench cases. The conclusions should be framed as average practical gains rather than uniform dominance.

Statistical reliability is underdeveloped. Many benchmark differences are small, and the paper does not report confidence intervals or multiple training seeds for the main LLM experiments. This is especially important for AIME-style benchmarks with small sample sizes and high variance.

The toy experiment is helpful pedagogically but somewhat artificial: the top-10 sampling restriction and single-logit update simplify the dynamics substantially, so it should be viewed as intuition rather than strong evidence about LLM training instability.

The manuscript says the code is publicly available, but the visible abstract does not include a URL. If this is not only an anonymization artifact, it weakens reproducibility. The paper also lacks a dedicated limitations section; the impact statement is acceptable but fairly generic and does not discuss possible failure modes such as over-preserving teacher uncertainty, dependence on entropy calibration, or risks inherited from teacher models.
